name: KY-011 two-colour LED module (red/green)
description: 5 mm bi-colour LED, red and green in one lens with a common cathode, on a 3-pin module. Each colour lights when its pin is driven high (forward voltage 2.0-2.5 V, 20 mA max); both on together gives yellow/orange, and PWM mixes shades. The module has NO current-limiting resistors fitted (the pads are empty), so each colour needs its own series resistor: 120 Ohm at 3.3 V, 220 Ohm at 5 V. Sold as: Joy-IT SEN-KY011LED / Keyes KY-011 2-colour 5 mm LED module from the 37-in-1 sensor kits, 3-pin header -, (middle, unlabelled = red), S (green).
eli5: One light that can glow red, green or both. Each colour has its own wire, and each wire needs a small resistor so the LED does not burn out.

pins.description: Common cathode of both LEDs: connect to GND

pins.name: MID
pins.description: Middle pin (unlabelled): red LED anode. High = red on. Needs a series resistor (120 Ohm at 3.3 V, 220 Ohm at 5 V); none is fitted on the board

pins.name: S
pins.description: Signal: green LED anode. High = green on. Needs a series resistor (120 Ohm at 3.3 V, 220 Ohm at 5 V); none is fitted on the board

supplierQuery: KY-011 two colour red green 5mm LED module common cathode
buildNotes: Header order (Joy-IT drawing): - (GND), middle unlabelled pin = red anode, S = green anode. Both LEDs share the cathode on -.

Always fit a series resistor in each colour line: 120 Ohm from a 3.3 V GPIO (about 10 mA), 220 Ohm from 5 V. The board's resistor pads are empty, so wiring a GPIO straight to MID or S overloads the LED and the pin.
On a Raspberry Pi Pico or Raspberry Pi keep each pin under about 12 mA: 120-220 Ohm is fine; 220 Ohm (about 5 mA) is still clearly bright.
Red and green on together look yellow/orange; PWM each pin (e.g. 1 kHz) to mix shades.
If the colours come out swapped, your clone has the LED legs the other way round: just swap the two signal wires in code.

example.code:
from machine import Pin
import time

# Each colour through its own 120-220 Ohm resistor.
red = Pin({MID}, Pin.OUT, value=0)    # middle pin = red anode
green = Pin({S}, Pin.OUT, value=0)    # S = green anode
while True:
    red.value(1)
    green.value(0)
    print('RED')
    time.sleep(1)
    red.value(0)
    green.value(1)
    print('GREEN')
    time.sleep(1)

test.title: The LED switches between red and green
